extracted.intended_audience: general readers, students, researchers, comedians, and anyone investigating insults, humor, or social interaction
extracted.subtask_description: Summarizing the types, functions, and social dynamics of insults (intentional/unintentional forms, categories, historical and entertainment uses) as described for a broad audience. Useful for analyzing or producing insulting remarks in social or comedic contexts.

rubrics_metrics.name: Insult (definition)
rubrics_metrics.description: An insult is an expression, statement, or behavior that is often deliberately disrespectful, offensive, scornful, or derogatory towards an individual or a group.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Insults can be intentional or unintentional, often aim to belittle, offend, or humiliate, and while they may include factual information, it is typically presented pejoratively to provoke a negative emotional response or socially undermine or discredit the target.

rubrics_metrics.name: Intent (intentional vs unintentional)
rubrics_metrics.description: Insults can be intentional or unintentional; unintentional insults arise from careless social actions and may be misinterpreted as deliberate.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples of unintentional insults include not tasting a host's dessert, comments about facial features or personal taste, use of stereotypes, jokes, or even walking away; these can have unintended negative impacts depending on recipient interpretation and context.

rubrics_metrics.name: Function / Purpose of insults
rubrics_metrics.description: Insults often aim to belittle, offend, humiliate, socially undermine, or discredit the target.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Understanding the intended function helps judge whether language is playful, manipulative, or malicious; function interacts with intent, recipient understanding, and social norms.

rubrics_metrics.name: Jocular exchange / comeback structure
rubrics_metrics.description: Insults can be part of jocular exchanges where one-liners set up potential comebacks, ripostes, toppers, or squelches in social interaction.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Goffman's examples (one-liner vs comeback) show how insult exchanges are structured in interaction and how they can be playful rather than malicious; consider potential for counter-riposte when composing or evaluating such remarks.

rubrics_metrics.name: Backhanded compliments (asteism)
rubrics_metrics.description: A backhanded (or left-handed) compliment or asteism is an insult disguised as, or accompanied by, a compliment, often intentionally condescending.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples: 'I did not expect you to ace that exam. Good for you.' or 'That skirt makes you look far thinner.' They belittle by framing praise as qualification or surprise; avoid if goal is genuine praise.

rubrics_metrics.name: Negging
rubrics_metrics.description: Negging is a type of backhanded compliment used for emotional manipulation or as a seduction method, coined and prescribed by pickup artists.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Often viewed as a straightforward insult rather than playful banter; proponents claim it's not an insult, but it typically undermines confidence and is generally unethical/manipulative in interpersonal contexts.

rubrics_metrics.name: Personal attacks
rubrics_metrics.description: A personal attack is an insult directed at an attribute of the person (honesty, character, integrity, or similar personal qualities).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Personal attacks are considered a fallacy in arguments (ad hominem) because they target the person rather than their argument; regulatory definitions (e.g., FCC personal attack rule) treat attacks on character as distinct and consequential.

rubrics_metrics.name: Sexuality-based insults and profanity
rubrics_metrics.description: Verbal insults often take phallic or pudendal form, include profanity, and may insult one's sexuality or extent of sexual activity.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Such insults can be particularly charged; modern examples include terms (e.g., 'incel') used in online harassment; be aware of cultural sensitivity and potential to escalate harm.

rubrics_metrics.name: Entertainment uses of insults
rubrics_metrics.description: Insults are used for entertainment in forms such as flyting, senna, Mozart's mocking pieces, poetry slams, dozens, roasts, diss tracks, battle rap, and insult comedy.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: In entertainment contexts, insults are often performative and accepted as part of genre conventions, but audience expectations and norms determine what is permissible or funny; historical examples show ritualized insult contests.

rubrics_metrics.name: Desmond Morris typology: 'Insult Signals' overview
rubrics_metrics.description: Desmond Morris argued that almost any action can operate as an insult signal if performed out of its appropriate context; he classes such signals in ten basic categories.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Treat Morris's categories as a typology for analyzing nonverbal and verbal insult signals and for designing or judging insulting acts in social or performative settings.

rubrics_metrics.name: Uninterest signals
rubrics_metrics.description: One of Morris's categories: actions that signal lack of interest and can be perceived as insulting when contextually misplaced.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples might include ignoring or turning away; assess whether the action's timing/context makes it an insult signal rather than neutral behavior.

rubrics_metrics.name: Boredom signals
rubrics_metrics.description: Morris category: actions that indicate boredom and can function as insults when directed at a person or group.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Yawning, checking the time, or distracted behavior can be insulting in contexts where attention is expected.

rubrics_metrics.name: Impatience signals
rubrics_metrics.description: Morris category: actions signaling impatience that may insult someone perceived as causing delay.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Exaggerated sighs or tapping can be insulting in social contexts requiring patience; context matters.

rubrics_metrics.name: Superiority signals
rubrics_metrics.description: Morris category: actions that communicate superiority and thereby insult implied inferiors.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Gestures or remarks that assert dominance or condescension function as insults and alter social dynamics.

rubrics_metrics.name: Deformed-compliment signals
rubrics_metrics.description: Morris category: compliments that are 'deformed' so as to function as insults (e.g., backhanded compliments).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Recognize when praise contains qualifying language that undermines the compliment and thus insults the recipient.

rubrics_metrics.name: Mock-discomfort signals
rubrics_metrics.description: Morris category: fabricated or exaggerated discomfort used to belittle or mock someone.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Feigning nausea, disgust, or distress near a person can be used to insult by implying they cause such reactions.

rubrics_metrics.name: Rejection signals
rubrics_metrics.description: Morris category: actions that convey rejection and thereby insult the rejected party.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Explicit refusals, exclusionary behavior, or dismissive gestures serve as social insults when aimed at individuals or groups.

rubrics_metrics.name: Mockery signals
rubrics_metrics.description: Morris category: actions that mimic or ridicule another, functioning as insults.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Imitation, parody, or exaggerated mimicry are common mockery forms; evaluate intent and audience norms for acceptability.

rubrics_metrics.name: Symbolic insults
rubrics_metrics.description: Morris category: symbolic actions or objects used to insult (e.g., gestures carrying meaning as insults).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples include the V sign used offensively in some cultures; symbolism and cultural meaning determine insult potency.

rubrics_metrics.name: Dirt signals
rubrics_metrics.description: Morris category: actions invoking dirt, contamination, or moral dirtiness to insult someone.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Associations with filth or uncleanliness (literal or moral) can be powerful insults; consider cultural taboos and stigma.

rubrics_metrics.name: Shakespeare's seven-fold degrees of insult
rubrics_metrics.description: Shakespeare (humorously) set up an insult-hierarchy of seven degrees: Retort Courteous; Quip Modest; Reply Churlish; Reproof Valiant; Countercheck Quarrelsome; Lie with Circumstance; Lie Direct.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use this hierarchy as a historical lens to classify escalating rhetorical severity from mild witty retort to outright lying; useful for literary or stylistic analysis.

rubrics_metrics.name: Context and perceptions (social norms determine insult status)
rubrics_metrics.description: What qualifies as an insult is determined by the individual social situation and by changing social mores — the same words/actions may be insulting in one context and affectionate in another.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Evaluate insults relative to intent, recipient's understanding, social setting, cultural references, and shifting norms; consider that erotic/affectionate uses between intimates may read differently than public uses.

rubrics_metrics.name: Historical and political usage of insults
rubrics_metrics.description: Insults have long been part of political speech and religious contexts (e.g., ancient Rome, Cadaver Synod), reflecting confrontational engagement or moral injunctions.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When analyzing insults in political or historical texts, consider rhetorical strategies, norms of public discourse, and the potential consequences (e.g., incitement, humiliation).
